title: Vanity of vanities
hookLine: vanity of vanities, all is vanity, a word meaning breath or vapor (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
tomorrow: is 'no new thing under the sun' bad news, or a comfort?

lines: HE LOOKS AT ALL OF IT.
cards: Bigger house, better job, one more trip: the next thing always promises to be the one that lasts.
The book of Ecclesiastes is told by a man the King James Bible calls the Preacher, a king in Jerusalem, who runs an experiment on his own life. "I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards," he says.
Then gardens, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers. Whatever his eyes wanted, he didn't keep from them. Then he stands back and looks at all of it.

teach.b: "And, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." Vanity is the King James word.
The Hebrew is hevel, and a standard Hebrew dictionary gives its first meaning as vapor, or breath.

It's even Abel's name in Genesis, the brother whose life was brief. So when the book opens, "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity," it isn't calling life worthless.
Hear it as: breath of breaths, all is breath. Brief. Real while it lasts, and impossible to hold.
Now the turn. Qoheleth, as the Preacher is called in Hebrew, doesn't stop at the empty shelves.

teach.h: EAT, DRINK: FROM THE HAND OF GOD.
teach.b: Again and again he comes back to the same counsel: there's nothing better than to eat and drink and find good in your work, and that too, he says, is from the hand of God.
In some Jewish communities the whole book is read aloud at Sukkot, the harvest festival kept in flimsy huts open to the sky.
The teaching, plainly: in this book of the Hebrew Bible, life is hevel, a breath. You can't grasp it. You can receive it, like bread while it's still warm.

how: Ecclesiastes (Qoheleth) is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament; in some Jewish communities it is read aloud during Sukkot, the festival spent in temporary huts.

o: breath or vapor: brief and impossible to hold
pride in your own looks and achievements
something useless that should be thrown away

games.q: the Preacher's experiment: tap the pairs.
p: a gift from the hand of God

s: it translates hevel: breath, vapor, something brief.
Abel's name in Genesis is the same Hebrew word, hevel
the brother whose life was brief carries the word for breath.
Ecclesiastes ends in despair: nothing is worth anything
it keeps returning to eating, drinking and finding good in work, as God's gift.

games.q: a friend finishes a huge project and says, 'what was the point? it's already over.' what's the Ecclesiastes answer?
o: it was breath: brief, real, a gift. eat a good meal and enjoy what you made.
there was no point, so there's no reason to start another one.
make the next one bigger, so it lasts and finally means something.
games.why: the Preacher tried bigger, and it was still hevel. his counsel is to receive it: eat, drink, find good in your work, from the hand of God.

practice: If there's a window, a mirror or a cold glass nearby, breathe on it gently and watch the cloud spread, then fade. Do it again, slowly, a few times. That's hevel: real for a moment, and already leaving.

wordCard.voice: Vanity of vanities: in Hebrew, hevel of hevels. Breath of breaths, the line that opens the book and comes back near its end.

orig.note: Hebrew hevel, breath or vapor: the word the King James Bible renders 'vanity'.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: breath, vapour, because brief isn't the same as worthless; it's a reason to taste it. Until tomorrow.
